reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Hepatobiliary involvement is a recognised complication of cystic fibrosis and, after cardiorespiratory disease, is an important non-pulmonary cause of morbidity and mortality
The characteristic hepatic lesion is focal biliary cirrhosis, which can progress to multilobular cirrhosis and portal hypertension, often with well-preserved synthetic function until late
Many patients have only mild, fluctuating enzyme abnormalities or hepatic steatosis without progressive disease, so liver function tests alone are insufficient for assessment
Portal hypertension with varices and splenomegaly may be the first clinical manifestation, sometimes before overt cirrhosis is apparent
Biliary complications include microgallbladder, gallstones, and a sclerosing-cholangitis-like biliary abnormality
The underlying defect is dysfunction of the CFTR chloride channel in biliary epithelium, leading to thick, inspissated bile and obstruction of small bile ducts
Ursodeoxycholic acid is commonly used to improve bile flow, and management otherwise focuses on nutrition, fat-soluble vitamins, and complications of portal hypertension
Liver transplantation, sometimes combined with lung transplantation, is considered for end-stage liver disease or decompensated portal hypertension
reference.pathophysiology: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene encoding a chloride channel expressed in the apical membrane of biliary (cholangiocyte) epithelium as well as in the airways and pancreas. Defective CFTR function reduces chloride and bicarbonate secretion into bile, producing viscous, poorly hydrated bile that becomes inspissated and obstructs the small intrahepatic bile ducts. The resulting bile stasis and retention of toxic bile constituents cause focal periportal inflammation and fibrosis, the lesion termed focal biliary cirrhosis. Over years this may coalesce into multilobular cirrhosis with portal hypertension, while synthetic function is often preserved until advanced disease. The same secretory defect underlies gallbladder abnormalities and gallstone formation.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of paediatric cirrhosis and portal hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Liver biochemistry with recognition that normal values do not exclude significant disease
Ultrasound and elastography to assess hepatic texture, fibrosis, and portal system
Upper endoscopy to screen for varices when portal hypertension is suspected
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography for biliary abnormalities
Liver biopsy in selected cases, recognising the patchy distribution of disease
redFlags: Hepatic decompensation with jaundice, ascites, or encephalopathy
Progressive cholestasis suggesting significant biliary obstruction
Rapid clinical deterioration warranting transplant assessment
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; many patients have mild, non-progressive hepatic involvement, while a subset develop multilobular cirrhosis and portal hypertension that contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality, with liver or combined liver-lung transplantation offering benefit in end-stage disease.
pitfalls: Relying on normal liver enzymes to exclude significant liver disease, given its patchy nature
Missing portal hypertension, which can precede obvious cirrhosis
Neglecting nutritional support and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation
Failing to consider transplantation in a patient whose overall condition might still permit it
